  • "Send to ▶" appears here (desktop shortcut, compressed folder, mail recipient and so on; its contents come from Windows).
  • "Share", "Pin to Quick access", "Open with..." and "Eject" are on the first level of the app's own menu (for a single file, a single folder, or an ejectable drive).
  • "Run as administrator" (.exe, .bat, .cmd, .msi, .com) and "Open file location" (for a shortcut it opens the folder containing the target and selects the target; for a search result it opens the folder containing the item and selects it) are also on the first level of the app's own menu.
  • Items registered the new Windows 11 way appear too. Apps can register right-click items the classic way or the new Windows 11 way, and the new way is normally shown only by File Explorer. Both are read and merged into one list, and an app registered both ways appears once.
  • Which items appear depends on the extension of what you selected, whether it is a folder, and whether you right-clicked empty space (the same rules File Explorer uses).

docs.title: Cloud menu (Box, SharePoint, OneDrive)
docs.text:
Always keep on this device / Free up space (as in File Explorer): right-click a single file or folder in a synced folder such as OneDrive (personal too) or Box Drive and they appear on the first level. Checking "Always keep on this device" downloads it and keeps it on the PC; unchecking it goes back to the default. "Free up space" makes it online-only again and frees the space on this PC. The sync app does the downloading and freeing in the background (for a folder, everything inside it too). Switching does not read the files.

Inside folders synced with Box Drive or SharePoint / OneDrive (work or school), two items can be used (elsewhere they are dimmed and cannot be clicked):

  • Cloud Menu ▶ calls the items cloud apps add to the right-click menu, such as "Share with Box" or "Version history".

  • Copy share link with path fetches the share link and puts it on the clipboard as both HTML and plain text. Pasted into Teams, Outlook, Slack and the like, each item name becomes a link; in Notepad and similar editors it reads "item name ( URL )". It has three layers: the parent folder's Box path, the parent folder's share URL, then each item name with its own link. Used on empty space, every item in the folder is listed. When it is done, "Box share info copied" appears and the pane flashes green.

    Since a Box Drive update, copying a link also opens Box's share window. Box has no setting to turn that off, so the app closes the window that this action opened (Box windows you opened yourself are left alone). If no share URL could be obtained you see "Box path copied only (share link unavailable)", and if none arrived within 20 seconds, "Could not get share link".

  • Box share link as two lines: in a Box folder, Shift + right-click to open the Explorer-compatible menu and choose "Share" → "Copy shared link". For the next 20 seconds the clipboard is watched, and as soon as Box writes the URL it is replaced with "line 1: Box path, line 2: share URL". When that happens the pane flashes green and the status bar shows "Box path and URL combined".

docs.title: Why the app's own menu opens instantly
docs.text:
• The app's own menu is built only from what the app already knows (the kind, number and location of what you selected). Nothing is asked of Windows, so there is no wait. The time it took is logged as [ContextMenu] shown in <ms>ms.
  • Items that have to be asked of Windows or other apps are fetched only when you hover over their submenu. With security software or cloud sync slowing things down, one fetch has been measured at 9.8 seconds, so the menu no longer fetches ahead on every right-click.
    • "OS standard menu ▶" fetches the classic and the Windows 11 items in parallel, so the wait is not doubled. If they are not ready within 6 seconds, "Still loading…" appears and it waits up to 30 seconds more. If there really are no items, "No items available" is shown.
    • "Cloud Menu ▶" waits up to 3 seconds when nothing is remembered yet.
  • Fetched items are remembered for 10 minutes (up to 20 entries), so opening the menu again on the same place and the same kind of file shows them at once. Empty results are not remembered, so the next open tries again.

docs.title: How the Explorer-compatible menu is shown
docs.text:
• The standard Windows menu is created by Windows on a dedicated thread. That thread runs aware of each monitor's scale (DPI), so the menu is drawn at the right size on every screen.
  • The menu is built for the folder containing the first selected item.
  • With Shift held while right-clicking, the normally hidden items (such as "Copy as path" and "Open PowerShell window here") appear too, as in File Explorer.
  • "Rename", "Delete" and "Properties" are handled by the app rather than Windows, so they behave just as they do from the app's own menu (the delete confirmation, the name input and so on).
  • Near the right or bottom edge of the screen, the menu shifts left or up to stay on screen.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Keyboard Shortcut Reference — change the keys shown in the menu
  • Archives — extracting and compressing
  • Text Comparison — compare two files side by side
  • Batch Rename — rename many items at once
  • Standard File Operations — copy, move and delete

docs.title: Drag & Drop
docs.text: The rules for copying and moving files by dragging, and what happens depending on where you drop them. It also covers how a copy proceeds after the drop (overwrite prompts and progress).

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
To do this Do this Copy or move to the other pane Drag files to the other pane Choose between copy and move Hold Ctrl to copy, Shift to move Create a shortcut Hold Alt (or Ctrl+Shift) while you drop Decide what to do when you drop Drag with the right button → "Copy here", "Move here" or "Create shortcut here" Send files up the tree Drop them on a folder name in the breadcrumb Exchange files with File Explorer and other apps Just drag (Outlook emails and browser addresses are accepted too) Open a place from Favorites or the history Drop the nav pane item on the file list

When a drag starts, the number of items you are carrying appears next to the cursor, as in "Drop 5 items to copy/move destination". Places you can drop on (folder rows and so on) are highlighted in the same color as a selected row.

docs.title: Starting a drag
docs.text:
• Select several items with Ctrl or Shift and drag to carry all of them. If you grab a row that is not selected, the selection is reset and only that row is carried (even if the mouse slides onto the next row after you grab it, the row you grabbed is the one that goes).
  • In the file list and the tab bar, a drag starts once the mouse moves 10px or more, so a slight wobble while clicking never moves anything by accident. The nav pane's tree, Favorites, history and so on use the Windows setting instead (usually 4px).
  • No drag starts while a right-click menu is open, or for 0.15 seconds after it closes.

The item count next to the cursor can be turned off with Effects → Show drag adorner (it is also hidden in lightweight mode).

docs.title: Where to drop
docs.text:
Drop on What happens A folder row in the file list Copy or move into that folder An empty part of the file list, or a file row Copy or move into the folder being shown A shortcut (.lnk) to a folder Copy or move into the folder it points to (copy vs. move is decided by where that folder is, too) An executable such as .exe Not copied: the program is started with the files passed to it (see Dropping on executables) A folder name in the breadcrumb Copy or move into that folder The tab bar Open the folder in a new tab (see Tabs). Dropping something that includes files on a tab header copies or moves it into that tab's folder (see "Dropping on a tab" below) A folder in the nav pane's tree Copy or move into that folder, by the same rules as the file list (see "Dropping on the tree" below) The nav pane's Favorites Add to Favorites (not while Favorites are locked) File Explorer, the desktop or another app Copied or moved by the receiving app's rules

Dropping on a folder that is out of view: while dragging, move the cursor to the top or bottom edge of the list (in the details view, over the column headers too) and the list scrolls that way on its own, faster the closer you are to the edge. Even with the cursor held still, the folder row that scrolls under it is highlighted, so release there to copy or move into that folder. Scrolling stops when you leave the list or release the button. Favorites and the tree in the nav pane work the same way.

Hover to open: while dragging, hold the cursor over a folder for about a second and it opens, as in File Explorer. Over a folder row in the file list, the list moves into that folder; over a branch in the nav pane tree, the branch expands; over a tab header, that tab comes to the front. You can work your way down to a deep folder and drop there. Once something opens, it won't open again until you move away and come back.

Where you can't drop: over the folder you are dragging, or a folder inside it, the cursor shows that you can't drop, as in File Explorer.

Dropping on the tree: copy or move is decided by the same rules as the file list (see "Copy or move" below), and a right drag shows the same menu. Dropping on the top or bottom edge of a folder row (a quarter of its height each) puts the items alongside that folder (into its parent) instead of into it. Dragging a folder within the tree works the same way. You cannot drop on the tree while it is locked. Items from the history, frequent folders, drives and Favorites cannot be dropped on the tree: they are there to open places, so drop them on Pane A or B.

Dropping on a tab: dropping something that includes files on a tab header copies or moves it into the folder open in that tab (by the same rules as the file list). Dropping only folders, or dropping on the tab bar away from a tab header, opens them in a new tab. Nothing is carried to a terminal tab or a server tab.

docs.title: Copy or move
docs.text:
With a left drag, the drop is decided in this order:

  • Alt held, or Ctrl and Shift held together → create a shortcut (a .lnk pointing to the original is made where you drop, as in File Explorer. When a server file or a server folder is involved a shortcut cannot be made, so it copies instead)
  • Ctrl held → copy
  • Shift held → move
  • Neither → move within the same drive; copy to another drive, a network share or a server (the same idea as File Explorer)

Pressing or releasing a key before you drop changes the cursor to match.

docs.title: Choosing with a right drag
docs.text:
Hold the right button while dragging, and a menu appears where you drop:

  • Copy here / Move here
  • Create shortcut here: creates a shortcut to the original (for example original name - Shortcut.lnk).

Clicking outside the menu does nothing. It works within a pane, across panes, on the breadcrumb and on the nav pane tree. The menu appears only for right drags that started inside the app (a right drag from File Explorer follows the same rules as a left drag).

When the right-click menu is set to "Explorer-compatible menu" (Settings → General → "Context Menu"), you get the same Windows menu as in File Explorer, including items added by apps such as 7-Zip or EXPLZH (for example "Create archive here").

  • The three items at the top (Copy here, Move here, Create shortcut here) are still carried out by the app itself, so the same-name check, the progress window and undo with Ctrl + Z all work. The bold item is the one a plain left drag would do (move on the same drive, copy to another drive)
  • App items are carried out by that app and cannot be undone with the app's Ctrl + Z
  • When you drop more than 200 items at once, only the three items are shown, without app items (for the same reason as in "Keeping right drags from stalling" below)
  • Dropping onto a server (FTP / SFTP) or Box folder shows the usual menu

With the default "App custom menu", an "Apps ▶" row appears under the three items. Press it to open a Windows menu with just the app items beside it. The three items still appear at once, and apps are loaded only when you press that row. If there are no app items, it says "No app items" (Windows' own zip items appear only when you drop a zip file).

docs.title: Receiving from outside
docs.text:
• Files from File Explorer: dropped on the file list or the breadcrumb, they are copied or moved by the same rules as inside the app.
  • Browser addresses: dropping the address bar or a link creates an Internet shortcut (.url) to that address.
  • Outlook emails and attachments: drop them, or paste with Ctrl + V, to save them in the current folder (emails become .msg files).

docs.title: Dropping items that open places
docs.text:
Items from the nav pane's Favorites, history, frequent folders, drives and tree, dropped on the file list, do not copy anything: they go to that folder. If search results are showing, the search is cleared first. Dropped on the tab bar, they open in a new tab. While you drag them, "Drop onto pane A or pane B" appears next to the cursor.

Items from Favorites, the history, frequent folders and drives are treated as bookmarks that point to a place. Dropped on File Explorer or the desktop, they create a shortcut, and the folder itself stays where it is. They cannot be dropped on the breadcrumb or the tree (they are never copied or moved). Tree items are real folders, so dropping one on File Explorer copies or moves it by File Explorer's rules.

docs.title: Dropping on executables
docs.text:
Dropping files on an .exe / .bat / .cmd / .com row, or on a Windows Script Host script (.js / .jse / .vbs / .vbe / .wsf), does not copy or move them. Instead, the program is started with the file paths passed as arguments. While you drag, that row is highlighted and the cursor changes to the shortcut shape, so you can tell it apart from a copy or move.

With several files selected, all their paths are passed together, and the program starts in its own folder. Because starting a program cannot be undone, you are asked first (choosing "No" neither copies nor moves anything). If there are so many files that the command line would be too long, nothing is started and you are told why.

.ps1 is not included (Windows drag and drop does not pass arguments to it either). Dropping on a .lnk to a folder copies or moves into the folder it points to. Files on a server (FTP / SFTP) cannot be passed as arguments.

docs.title: How copy or move is decided
docs.text:
• "The same drive" means the start of the path (C: or \\server\share) is the same, ignoring letter case. The actual disk is not checked, so a different disk attached as a folder (a mounted folder or a junction) counts as the same drive.
  • Server (FTP / SFTP) folders always count as "somewhere else". Transfers with a server only support copying, so a move is done as a copy and you are told that the original was left in place. Files cannot be carried directly from one server to another.

docs.title: After the drop
docs.text:
Copies and moves dropped on the file list, the breadcrumb, the nav pane tree or a tab header all run through the app's own transfer engine.

  1. Count first: it counts how many files there are and how big they are. If you are trying to put a folder inside itself, it stops here.
  2. Progress window: General → "File operations" → Copy progress window in Settings chooses whether a window with speed and time remaining appears: Always show (the default) / Only for large transfers (50 files or 50 MB) / Never (the bar at the bottom left only). Closing the window does not stop the transfer; the bar at the bottom left takes over. When everything succeeds the window closes after 1 second (tick "Close when done" in its footer to have it close straight away).
  3. Name clashes: folders with the same name are merged (what was already in the destination stays), and only files with the same name are asked about. The "File Conflict" dialog offers Replace, Skip, Keep both, Keep newer and Keep larger. By default one answer covers every clash; clear "Do the same for the remaining N" to decide one file at a time (see File Conflict Dialog).

  4. Several at a time: files are carried in parallel, half as many as your CPU has cores (2 to 8). After 3 failures in a row, the transfer stops.

  5. Moving something into the folder it is already in is skipped. Copying into the same folder makes "original name - Copy" without asking.

docs.title: Keeping right drags from stalling
docs.text: For a right drag, a Windows shell item is created for each file so the drop behaves like File Explorer's. That takes time per file: right-dragging 1,284 files in a cloud-synced folder froze the window for 1.5–1.9 seconds. So shell items are created for up to 200 files, and beyond that only the list of paths is handed over.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Address Bar and Breadcrumb — dropping on the breadcrumb
  • Tabs — dragging tabs, dropping on the tab bar
  • File Operations — copy, move and delete
  • Nav Pane — the tree, Favorites and history
  • FTP/SFTP — exchanging files with a server

docs.title: Standard File Operations
docs.text:
The following operations are available via right-click menu or keyboard shortcuts.

By default, an app-specific lightweight menu appears instantly, providing quick access to open, copy, delete, rename, favorites, and index search. See "Context Menu" for details.

  • Copy, Cut, Paste: Same as Windows standard (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V).

    After the operation, focus remains on the file list. After copy/cut, focus stays on the operated items. After paste, focus moves to the pasted files.

    After pasting, the list auto-scrolls to the file for immediate visibility. Focus is maintained even after folder monitoring auto-refresh and is not stolen by the other pane.

  • New folder: Press Ctrl+Shift+N and a folder named "New folder" ("New folder (2)" and so on if the name is taken) is created in the current folder right away, selected, with the rename dialog open. Type a name and press OK to keep it; cancel and the new folder is removed again. "New folder" in the right-click menu works the same way.

    In a server (FTP / SFTP) folder, you are asked for the name first and the folder is created afterwards.

  • Rename: Press F2 or use the menu. A dedicated rename dialog appears.

    • File vs folder: For files, the file name and extension are displayed separately and can be edited independently (preventing accidental extension changes). For folders, the entire name is editable.
    • Changing the extension: as in File Explorer, it asks first, warning that the file might become unusable. Answer No and the name stays as it was (the same applies when renaming in place in the list; case-only changes and names like .gitignore are not asked about).
    • Dialog caching: Cached as a lightweight shared window within the app for instant display.
    • Template input buttons:
      • 3 date buttons (YYYYMMDD / YYYYMMDD_ / _YYYYMMDD): Insert today's date instantly.
      • 2 context buttons (parent folder name / YYYYMMDD_議事ログ_ParentFolderName): Quickly input template names using the current folder name (hidden at drive root). The second one always inserts the Japanese word 「議事ログ」 ("meeting log"), whatever the display language.
      • Custom buttons: The "+" at the end (Add current input as a custom button) keeps the name you are typing as a button, so you can enter it again with one click. Remove one you no longer need with "Delete this button" in its right-click menu.
    • Input history popup: Focusing the text box automatically displays previously used rename values for reuse (up to 100 entries, sorted by most recently used).
    • Characters that can't be used are left out: As in File Explorer, typing \ / : * ? " < > | enters nothing, and when you paste text those characters are removed and only the rest is entered. When characters are removed, "A file name can't contain any of the following characters" appears below the box for a few seconds. The same applies when you rename an item in place in the file list.
    • Real-time input validation: Validates the name 0.3 seconds after you stop typing. If the name is a reserved name (CON, PRN, NUL, etc.) or ends with a dot or a space, a warning appears and the OK button is disabled. If a file or folder with the same name already exists in the same folder, a warning also appears, but the OK button remains enabled. Changing only upper or lower case (a.txt to A.txt) shows no warning, because it is the same file.
    • Renaming in place in the list (click a selected row again slowly, when turned on in Settings): Enter commits, Esc cancels, and clicking elsewhere commits. Tab commits and starts renaming the next row, and Shift+Tab the previous row, as in File Explorer. It stops at the first and last rows.

  • Delete: Press Delete. Items are sent to the Recycle Bin. If "Show confirmation dialog when deleting files" is on in the Control Deck (the default), a confirmation dialog appears first. When something would be deleted permanently instead (files on a network, or files too large for the Recycle Bin), Windows warns you regardless of the setting.

    • Ctrl+Z undoes it: a delete to the Recycle Bin is undone by restoring the items from the Recycle Bin to where they were. If something with the same name went into the Recycle Bin several times, the one from that delete is restored. If something with the same name is already in the original location, it isn't overwritten and you're told it couldn't be restored. Items deleted permanently (Shift+Delete), or deleted in a network location (which has no Recycle Bin), can't be restored.

  • Create shortcut: Creates a shortcut to the selected item in the current folder. The name follows File Explorer, such as "report.xlsx - Shortcut.lnk", and a duplicate gets a number starting from "(2)". The new shortcut is selected, so you can rename it right away with F2.

  • Show properties: Displays the standard Windows properties dialog.

  • Open in Explorer: Opens the current folder in Windows Explorer.

  • Process display on file operation error: When a rename, delete, copy, move, or drag & drop operation fails because another application is using the file, the error message shows the name of the process locking the file (e.g., "EXCEL is using this file, so the operation could not be completed").

  • Copying or moving to places that need permission (such as C:\Program Files): if some items could not be written because you lack permission, the status bar shows a notice with a "Continue as administrator" button. Clicking it shows Windows' confirmation (UAC) once and carries all of those items again (like File Explorer's "Continue"; Windows asks about name conflicts). This retry cannot be undone with Ctrl+Z. The button does not appear when other reasons (file in use, not enough space) are mixed in, or when ransomware protection blocked the operation.

    The Windows Restart Manager API is used to identify the process, making it immediately clear which application needs to release the file. Appropriate messages are also shown for insufficient access permissions or disk space.

docs.title: Rubber Band Selection
docs.text:
You can select a rectangle area by dragging on empty space in both detail and icon views.

  • Press and hold the left mouse button on an empty area and drag to draw a selection rectangle adorner; items inside are selected.
  • Where to start dragging: In detail view, start from the narrow strip along the left edge of the list (it runs down from the left of the column headers). In icon view, start from the gaps between cards. You don't have to start on top of a row or card, even when you only want to pick two items in the middle of the list. Right-clicking this empty space opens the folder background menu.
  • Ctrl + Drag: Keeps the existing selection and toggles the items you enclose (selected ones are deselected, unselected ones are selected).
  • Shift + Drag: Keeps the existing selection and adds the items you enclose, as in File Explorer.
  • Auto-scroll at edges: When the mouse reaches a list edge, the list auto-scrolls while the rectangle selection continues.
  • Rubber band is inactive during keyboard operation mode (requires mouse movement to resume).

docs.title: Selecting with check boxes
docs.text:
Turn on Use check boxes to select items under Display in the settings to pick several items with the mouse alone, like File Explorer's "Use check boxes to select items" (off by default).

  • Where they appear: On every item, to the left of the name in detail view and at the top left of the card in icon view. Selected items have a tick.
  • Clicking a check box: Adds or removes just that item (the same as Ctrl + click). The rest of the selection stays. Dragging, opening and renaming do not start from a check box, and a folder whose check box you click does not open even with "Open folders with a single click" on.
  • Select all: The check box in the Name header in detail view selects everything. Click it again when everything is selected to clear all. It shows a dash when only some items are selected.
  • Clicking an item's name or icon, clicking empty space, and the keyboard all work as before (clicking a name selects only that item, as in File Explorer).
  • Check boxes do not appear in search results or in the nav pane lists.

docs.title: File Conflict Dialog (same-name handling)
docs.text:
When a same-name file exists during copy/move, a dedicated conflict dialog appears, offering 5 actions. The size and modified date of the source and the existing file are shown side by side, each with its picture (a thumbnail for images, an icon otherwise), so you can compare them (the pictures appear a moment after the dialog opens; none is shown for cloud files that are online-only, FTP/SFTP, or items inside an archive).

Action Behavior Replace Overwrite the existing file with the source Skip Leave that file out Keep both Leave the existing file alone and place the source under another name. The name is chosen automatically as "name - Copy" ("name - Copy (2)" and so on if that is taken), and you can edit it while deciding one file at a time Keep newer Keep whichever was modified more recently (replace if the source is newer, otherwise skip) Keep larger Keep whichever is larger (replace if the source is larger, otherwise skip)
  • With Keep newer and Keep larger, files with the same date or size are skipped.
  • Copying or moving onto a folder with the same name merges the two folders, as in File Explorer. Files and folders that were only in the destination stay. Only files that end up with the same name inside are asked about, and the dialog shows where each one is, counted from the destination folder (such as "Photos > 2024 > a.jpg"). When a file and a folder share a name, nothing is overwritten even if you choose Replace; both are kept. When moving, source folders left empty are removed, and folders that still hold skipped items stay.
  • Moving into a folder above it with the same name (for example, moving the B inside A\B directly under A) also merges its contents into the upper B, as in File Explorer. If the moved B itself contains another B, that one is not merged into itself; it is kept under a "keep both" name. Copying into a folder above it is not possible, because the copy would be written into the folder being read; the no-drop cursor appears while you drag
  • When several files clash, one answer applies to all of them by default ("Do the same for the remaining N" is on). Clear the checkbox to be asked about each file in turn. The heading shows which one you are on (for example "2 of 5"), and ticking the box again partway through applies that answer to the rest. Keep newer and Keep larger compare each file, so they always apply to all remaining files regardless of the checkbox.
  • Renaming the kept copy: while you decide one file at a time (including when only one file clashes), the "Name for the copy when keeping both" box holds the name it will get. Edit it and press Keep both, or press Enter in the box, to use that name. Names with characters Windows does not allow, or the same name as the existing file, cannot be used. If the name has been taken by the time the file is copied, a number is added instead of overwriting.
  • Move between the buttons with ← → (or Tab) and press Enter; Replace is selected when the dialog opens.
  • Esc or × cancels the whole operation, including the remaining files. Progress and results appear in the copy progress window (or the bar at the bottom left if you turned the window off).
  • Until you answer, the dialog stays in front of Zenith Filer's windows, but it no longer covers other apps when you switch to them, so you can compare the files in Explorer.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Opening folders, Back / Forward / Up, the PC view, jumping to common places, and moving between Zenith Filer and File Explorer. To move with the breadcrumb or by typing a path, see Address Bar and Breadcrumb.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
To… Do this Go into a folder Double-click, or press Enter Go back / go forward again Alt + ← / Alt + → (or the mouse side buttons) Go up one level Backspace or Alt + ↑ Pick another drive "Up" from a drive root → PC view Jump to a usual place Home, Desktop and Downloads on the toolbar (hidden at first; see "Jumping to common places" below) Move to and from File Explorer Open the current folder in Explorer (Ctrl + Shift + X) / bring in the folders open in Explorer

The navigation buttons sit together on row 1 of the pane header (the action row). Going back or up puts the focus on the folder you just came out of, so you never lose your place, even when moving around with the keyboard alone.

docs.title: Open, Back, Forward, Up
docs.text:
• Open folder: Double-click or press Enter.

  • Go back: Toolbar "←" button, Alt + ←, or the mouse "back" side button.

    In the returned list, the previously entered folder is focused, allowing continued arrow-key navigation from that position.

  • Go forward: Toolbar "→" button, Alt + →, or the mouse "forward" side button.

  • Pick from the history: Right-click the toolbar "←" or "→" button to list the back or forward history, nearest first (up to 15 entries). Choosing one goes straight there without loading the folders in between (as in File Explorer).

  • Go up one level: Toolbar "↑" button, Backspace or Alt + ↑.

    In the returned list, the previously entered folder is focused, allowing continued arrow-key navigation.

    Executing "Up" at a drive root (e.g., C:\) navigates to a "PC" view listing all drives.

You can change the keys under Settings > Shortcut Keys. With the "Explorer style" preset, Backspace becomes Back and only Alt + ↑ is Up.

docs.title: PC view
docs.text:
A virtual top-level hierarchy above drive roots.

  • All drives on the PC (local disks, network drives, removable disks, etc.) and devices such as phones and cameras are listed; double-click or press Enter to navigate to a drive root. The "Type" column shows the kind of drive (local, removable, network and so on) and the "Size" column its total capacity with a thin bar showing how full it is (as in File Explorer, the bar turns to the warning colour above 90%; hover over it to see the free space). The bar is shown for local and removable drives only, not network drives (a disconnected one can keep you waiting).

  • A "PC" segment is always displayed at the beginning of the breadcrumb list, and clicking it navigates to the PC view. Clicking the "›" to the right of "PC" lets you pick a drive from a list instead.

  • Typing "PC" in the address bar and pressing Enter also navigates there.

  • There is nothing above the PC view, so "Up" does nothing there.

docs.title: Jumping to common places
docs.text:
On a new installation (where the toolbar's number of buttons is "Fewer"), the Home, Desktop and Downloads buttons and the two buttons under "Moving to and from File Explorer" below are hidden. Set "Number of buttons" to "Standard" under Settings → Toolbar to show them (see File Panes).

  • Add to favorites: Press the ★ button at the right end of the address bar to register the currently displayed folder to favorites.
  • Navigate to home: Click the home icon on the toolbar to navigate to the home folder set in app settings. If not configured, Pane A goes to Desktop and Pane B goes to Downloads.
  • Navigate to Desktop: Click the monitor icon on the toolbar to navigate to the Desktop folder.
  • Navigate to Downloads: Click the download icon on the toolbar to navigate to the Downloads folder.
  • Copy path: Click the copy icon on the right end of the address bar to copy the current folder's full path to the clipboard.

docs.title: Moving to and from File Explorer
docs.text:
• Open in Explorer: Click the open-folder icon on the toolbar to open the currently displayed folder in Windows Explorer (Ctrl + Shift + X).

  • Import Explorer folder: Click the import icon on the toolbar (right of the open-folder icon) to import folders from currently open Windows Explorer windows. The Recycle Bin is not a folder and can't be imported; a File Explorer window showing it is left open, and you are told why (you can also open the Recycle Bin from the Tree view in the nav pane).

    Imported folders are always shown in new tabs.

    • If there is only 1: opens in a new tab and the Explorer window closes.
    • If there are 2 or more: a selection dialog lets you choose which to import; selected folders each open in new tabs and the corresponding Explorer windows close.

docs.title: Keeping the list up to date
docs.text:
• Refresh: Press F5 (or Ctrl + R) or click the toolbar refresh button (folder changes are auto-detected, but manual refresh is also available).

    The keys and the button work in Details view and icon views alike.

    When folder monitoring connection is lost on network drives, automatic reconnection is attempted with exponential backoff (1s → 2s → 4s → … up to 30s). Reconnection progress is notified in the status bar ("Network disconnection detected. Attempting reconnection..." → "Folder monitoring resumed" on success).

    After reaching the maximum (10 attempts), "Folder monitoring has stopped. Press F5 to refresh" is displayed; F5 or the refresh button enables manual reconnection.

docs.title: From opening a folder to seeing its list
docs.text:
1. Check that the folder exists: this waits up to 2 seconds (0.3 seconds for folders on a network). Navigation stops only when the folder is confirmed missing; if the check cannot tell in time, the folder is opened anyway, so a slow network never blocks you just because the check was slow. The answer is remembered for 0.8 seconds, so opening the same folder again right away skips the check.
  2. Push onto Back: the folder you were in goes onto the Back history, and Forward is cleared (the same idea as a web browser).
  3. Read the contents on a background thread: the window never freezes. Only one load runs at a time; if you move somewhere else mid-load, the newer request reads the latest location.
  4. Show the whole list at once: sorting is finished in the background, then the list is swapped in one go. Rows are only created for what is visible on screen, so drawing stays light even for folders with tens of thousands of items.
  5. Icons, types and thumbnails follow: items first appear with a generic icon for their extension, then the real icons and type names are filled in on a background thread, 200 at a time. Thumbnails and large icons are fetched only for the part of the list you can see.
  6. Re-attach the folder watcher: files added or removed from outside show up in the list automatically. Changes are gathered for 0.12 seconds at a time, and the list is refreshed at most once every 0.5 seconds (2.5 seconds for cloud-synced folders), so a sync tool rewriting many files cannot keep the list flickering.

docs.title: The Back / Forward history
docs.text:
• History is kept per tab and records only folder locations — not which file was selected or where you had scrolled to.
  • It lives in memory only, and is lost when the tab closes or the app exits. A tab made with "Duplicate tab" starts with no history.
  • On Back and Up, the app remembers the folder you are leaving and focuses it once the new list has loaded. If you click in the list or press a key while it is still loading, your action wins and the focus is left alone.

docs.title: How the PC view lists drives
docs.text:
• The list of drives is built on a background thread by asking Windows. Drives that are not ready (such as a card reader with no card) are left out.
  • Display names (such as "Local Disk (C:)") are the same ones File Explorer shows, taken from Windows.
  • A disconnected network drive can delay the list while it waits for a reply. The window does not freeze, so other tabs and panes stay usable.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Address Bar and Breadcrumb — move with the breadcrumb or by typing a path
  • Tabs — open folders in new tabs
  • Favorites — register folders you use often
  • Nav Pane — move from the Tree or Browse History
  • Keyboard Shortcut Reference — change the navigation keys

docs.title: Ring Launcher
docs.text:
Pick a feature by direction from a ring that appears around the cursor. Press the left and right mouse buttons together and it appears wherever you are (Ctrl+Shift+Space works too; the key can be changed under Settings → "Shortcuts").

It is a feature you use while holding the mouse, so summoning it takes nothing but the mouse. Single left and right clicks behave exactly as before — only the moment a second button goes down is examined, and the first press is always passed straight through.

Where the command palette is the route that reaches every feature by name, this is the route that reaches the eight you use most without moving your hand. Both entry points share the same catalogue of features.

  • Hold, flick toward one, and let go — it runs right there. Flicking far is fine: the ring stays live past its outer edge, so only the direction matters. Let go without moving and the ring simply stays open.
  • Release straight away and the ring stays open. Pick with a click, 1–8, the numeric keypad (where the key's position is the direction — 8 is up, 6 is right, 3 is lower right), or the arrow keys plus Enter. When you summoned it with the key, holding it and pressing 3 is the quickest route of all.
  • To close: Esc, the same gesture again, a click outside the ring, or switching to another app.
  • The file list underneath never starts a drag while the ring is up. Moving the mouse with a button still held affects neither the selection nor any drag.
  • Your keyboard focus never moves. You can be in the nav pane tree or midway through typing in the search box and carry straight on afterwards.
  • It opens while you are typing in the terminal too — with the two buttons or with the key. In that case the digits and arrows go to the terminal, so you pick with the mouse (the number labels are hidden as well).
  • You can see what is currently on. Features with an on/off state, such as the split modes and the nav panes, light a thin outer arc the moment the ring opens.
  • The contents are yours to change under Settings → "Ring Launcher" (see All Control Deck settings). Summoning the ring and its eight starting entries are available to everyone.
  • The look and motion can be chosen from five presets, and how names are shown from three (Settings → "Ring Launcher" → "Design"). These are available to everyone too.

Light and motion

The ring moves by one rule: there is a single light, and it follows your hand — by the shortest way round, just a beat behind.

  • Opening: a seed of light glows in the centre, then a thin line runs around the rim in both directions from the direction you last chose and meets itself on the far side. The slots bloom as the line passes, so your eye lands first where your hand already knows to go.
  • Pointing: the light on the rim swings round to wherever you point, taking the shorter way. Move quickly and it stretches out with a trail; stop and it settles to the width of the slot. Shift your hand a little inside a slot and the light leans that way too. A thin needle on the edge of the centre circle faces the same direction, and the name of what you are pointing at slides in from that side to the centre. Names shrink to fit the circle and longer ones wrap to two or three lines.
  • Choosing: the chosen slot dips for an instant, the light swells, and a ripple spreads from the spot you chose. The other slots fold into the centre, farthest first.
  • Waiting: point at nothing for a moment and a faint light makes a single lap of the rim (Standard, Bloom and Pulse designs only).
  • The ring itself — the slots and the rim — stays still however you move your hand. Even when you trace all the way round the rim, only the light moves.
  • With "Enable file list effects" turned off under Settings → "Effects", or in lightweight mode, the light does not travel; it simply appears where you point. The Slate design is just as quiet.

How names are shown

Option What you see Horizontal labels (default) Names sit next to the icons in horizontal text, cut to fit inside the ring; the full name appears in the centre Icons only The ring shows only slightly larger icons, and the name of whatever you point at appears large in the centre Curved text Smaller text curves along the outer edge of the ring; text on the lower half still reads left to right

A second ring (multi-level mode, Pro)

When eight is not enough, a second ring can sit beyond a slot (set the mode to Multi-level, then press [Sub-ring] on the Assignment tab).

  • The parent ring stays where it is and the child blooms outside it, starting from the slot you opened. Keep the buttons held, flick to the entry, then flick further out and release: your finger never stops on the way to the deeper feature.
  • You never lose sight of where you came from. The parent you came through stays lit, the centre shows the parent's name small with the child you are pointing at below it, and the light passes from the parent ring out to the child ring. A small outward mark sits on every slot that leads somewhere.
  • While the buttons are held, there are only two ways to close a child — return to the centre, or move to a different slot. A shaky hand will not make the rings flicker.
  • Once the ring is left standing, moving the pointer never switches rings. The child blooms outside the parent, so heading straight for the entry you want always takes you across another slot; switching there would force you to arc around the rim instead. To open a different slot, click it (or use 1–8 / Enter). Passing back through the centre does not close it either.
  • With the ring left open, 1–8, a click, or Enter goes down, and BackSpace, a click in the centre, or a right-click goes back up. Esc and a click outside the ring both close the whole thing from any depth — clicking outside means "never mind", so it never just folds one layer away.
  • Nesting goes two levels deep (8 + 7×8 = up to 64 entries).
  • Assignments can be saved under a name ("Saved definitions" on the Assignment tab). "Save the current assignment" stores them and "Apply" swaps them in. The author's "Preset (single layer, 8 slots)" and "Preset (two layers, 64 items)" are listed too, so you can try a two-level layout straight away.
  • If you do not use sub-rings, the ring's size and feel are completely unchanged. It only grows once a sub-ring is attached, so near a screen edge the ring is pulled inward (and the cursor moves to its centre with it).

The starting layout gives each direction a meaning.

Direction Feature Upper left Single pane Up Side-by-side panes Upper right Stacked panes Left Show / hide the left nav pane Right Show / hide the right nav pane Lower left New folder Down Working sets Lower right Quick Jump

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text: Panes A and B can each keep several folders open as tabs. This article covers opening, closing, switching and rearranging tabs, and what comes back when you start the app again.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
To do this Do this Open a new tab "+", Ctrl + T, or double-click an empty part of the tab bar Open a folder in a background tab Middle-click the folder in the file list Open in a new tab from the nav pane or the breadcrumb Middle-click an item in Favorites, History and similar lists, or a folder in the breadcrumb Close a tab "×", Ctrl + W, or middle-click the tab Switch tabs Click, or Ctrl + Tab / Ctrl + Shift + Tab Pick a tab from a list The list button, or Ctrl + Shift + A Reorder tabs or move one to the other pane Drag the tab Move several tabs at once Ctrl- or Shift-click tabs to select them, then drag Keep a tab from being closed by accident Right-click → "Lock" Tell your tabs apart Right-click → "Name, note and color…"

Each pane has its own row of tabs, and each tab keeps its own Back / Forward history until you close it. When you quit, the same tabs come back the next time you start the app.

docs.title: Opening
docs.text:
• New tab: click "+" on the right of the tab bar, press Ctrl + T, or double-click an empty part of the tab bar. A new tab opens the pane's home folder and is added at the right end (with no home folder set, Pane A uses Desktop and Pane B uses Downloads). It uses the same view mode and icon size as the tab you were looking at.
  • Open a folder in a new tab: middle-click a folder in the file list to open it in a background tab. The folder you are looking at stays put, so, as with middle-clicking links in a browser, you can queue up several places at once (turn this off with General → Open folders in a new tab with middle-click in Settings). The right-click "Open in new tab" does the same.
  • Open in a new tab from the nav pane or the breadcrumb: middle-click an item in a nav pane list (Favorites, History, Frequently Used, the folder tree, Drives, Recent Files, Remote and Box) or a folder in the breadcrumb to open it in a new tab in the active pane and switch to that tab. Unlike a double-click, the current tab is not replaced. For Recent Files, the folder containing the file opens. Middle-clicking an entry in Search History or Saved Searches opens the current folder in a new tab and runs the search there. All of these are turned off by the same setting (Open folders in a new tab with middle-click).
  • Drop a folder on the tab bar: drag a folder onto the tab bar and release it to open it in a new tab. Dragging from Favorites, the folder tree or the history works too. If you drop several folders, only the first one opens, and files are ignored.
  • Terminal tab: the button to the right of "+" opens a terminal as a tab, working in the current folder (if the folder cannot be used for that, such as a folder on a server, it starts in your user folder).

docs.title: Closing
docs.text:
• Click the tab's "×", press Ctrl + W, or middle-click the tab. Middle-click closing also works on the terminal tabs in the nav pane.
  • Locked tabs and the last tab left in a pane are never closed.
  • After closing, the tab to the right of the closed one is selected (or the one to the left, if you closed the rightmost tab).
  • Reopen a closed tab: Ctrl + Shift + T (as in a browser). The folder tab you closed last comes back in its old position with the same view, name, note and color. Press again to go further back (up to 20 tabs until the app closes; terminal tabs cannot be reopened). For combinations you use all the time, save a working set to bring them all back at once.
  • Close several at once: right-click a tab → "Close other tabs" or "Close tabs to the right". Locked tabs stay open.

docs.title: Switching
docs.text:
• Click a tab, or press Ctrl + Tab for the next tab and Ctrl + Shift + Tab for the previous one. At either end it wraps around.

  • Tab list: the list button at the right end of the tab bar, or Ctrl + Shift + A, lists the current pane's tabs.

    • Click one, or pick it with ↑ ↓ and press Enter, to switch to it.
    • Close a tab with its "×", or by picking it and pressing Delete or Ctrl + W (locked tabs have no "×").
    • Esc or a click outside the list closes it.
    • From either pane, Ctrl + Shift + Alt + 1 opens Pane A's list and Ctrl + Shift + Alt + 2 opens Pane B's.

    You can change these keys in Settings → Shortcut Keys.

docs.title: Reordering and moving to the other pane
docs.text:
• Reorder: drag a tab left or right (the drag starts once you move 10px).

  • To the other pane: drag a tab onto the other pane's tab bar to move it to where you drop it. The tab's right-click menu offers the same and more:

    • Move to other pane moves the tab itself, and its Back / Forward history goes with it.
    • Duplicate to other pane (Ctrl + N) opens the same folder in a new tab in the other pane and leaves the original where it is.
    • Duplicate tab (Ctrl + Shift + D) opens the same folder in a new tab in the same pane. It acts on the tab you right-clicked, so you can duplicate a tab that is not selected.

    A duplicated tab starts with no Back / Forward history. Moving or duplicating to the other pane while only one pane is shown switches to two panes. - Move several tabs at once (as in a browser): Ctrl-click a tab to add it to the selection (again to remove it), or Shift-click to select every tab from the open tab to the clicked one. The open tab does not change. Every tab in the selected group is outlined in the same color as a focused input box (the open tab too, while other tabs are selected), and the tabs you added are lightly tinted in that color. Drag any of the selected tabs and they all move together in order, whether you reorder within the pane or drop them on the other pane. "Move to other pane" on the right-click menu also moves all the selected tabs. A plain click on a tab clears the selection

docs.title: Naming, noting and coloring a tab
docs.text:
Right-click a tab → "Name, note and color…" and a small box opens under the tab. It works on folder tabs and terminal tabs alike.

  • Name: becomes the tab title (instead of the folder name). Useful when several folders share a name, or to label tabs by task
  • Note: shown together with the name and location when you hover over the tab
  • Color: adds a colored band to the tab (the same 7 colors as Favorites color tags)
  • Nothing is stored: they go away when you close the tab, and they move with the tab to the other pane. Details such as keys are the same as in Terminal

docs.title: Locking, and adding all tabs to Favorites
docs.text:
• Lock: right-click a tab → "Lock". A locked tab shows a padlock instead of "×" and cannot be closed. Right-click → "Unlock" to undo it. Locks are kept the next time you start the app.
  • Add all tabs in this pane to favorites: choose it from a tab's right-click menu to add the folders of every tab in that pane to Favorites, grouped in a new virtual folder. You enter the folder name and an optional description before it is saved. Folders that no longer exist or are already in Favorites are skipped.

docs.title: Changing how tabs look
docs.text:
These are in the Tab section of Settings.

Setting Options Tab Width Fixed Width (tabs shrink to fit their name, up to the fixed width size below) / Auto-adjust to Folder Name (up to 600px) Fixed Width Size 100, 120, 150 (default), 200 or 250px Tab Wrapping Single Row (Scroll) / Multiple Rows (Wrap) Tab Row Height Sync When wrapping, keeps the tab bars of Panes A and B the same height so the address bars line up Tab List Integration Hides the A/B tab bars while the Tab Management view is shown in the nav pane

Tab text size is under Display → Tab text, and the switching animation (the underline catching up from the previous tab with a trail of light; the contents never move) can be turned off with Effects → Enable tab operation animations.

docs.title: What comes back at startup
docs.text:
• Tabs are saved per pane to settings.json when you quit: each tab's folder, whether it is locked and what kind it is (folder or terminal), plus the selected tab, whether the address bar was a text box, the view mode, icon size and sort order, and the pane's home folder.
  • Search result tabs come back as ordinary folder tabs (the search is not run again).
  • Only the tab that was selected reads its folder right away. The others read theirs the first time you switch to them, so keeping many tabs open does not slow down startup.
  • With General → Restore previous tabs on startup turned off, each pane starts with a single tab on its home folder.

docs.title: Remembering each folder's view
docs.text: When General → Auto-restore folder display settings is on (the default), the sort order, view mode, icon size and "folders first" you used in a folder are remembered when you leave it and applied the next time you open that folder, in any tab. Folders not opened for 180 days are forgotten.

docs.title: What makes switching fast
docs.text:
• The views of the 6 most recently used tabs are kept as they are. Switching back shows them without rebuilding anything, so the selected files and scroll position are exactly as you left them. When you switch to a seventh tab, the view of the tab you have not looked at for the longest is let go (never the selected tab or a terminal tab). A tab whose view was let go rebuilds it the next time you switch to it.
  • Hidden tabs keep watching their folders. When files appear or disappear, the tab just marks itself as needing a reload and reloads when you switch to it, so hidden tabs do not keep reloading and slow down the one you are working in.
  • Back / Forward history is kept in memory per tab and is gone once you close the tab or quit the app.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Navigation — Back, Forward and Up
  • Address Bar and Breadcrumb — go somewhere by typing a path
  • Nav Pane — handle the A/B tabs together in the Tab Management view
  • Working Sets — save a combination of tabs and bring it back
  • Keyboard Shortcuts — change the tab keys

docs.title: Archives (Extract and Compress)
docs.text:
Open and create archives such as ZIP without leaving the app. Everything lives under Archive ▶, at the top level of the right-click menu.

Its contents swap depending on what you selected. With only archives selected you get the extraction commands; with anything else you get the compression commands. Showing both at all times would mean reading the list every time to work out which half currently applies. If even one non-archive is mixed into the selection, you get the compression side.

Where the destination is already decided, the resulting folder or file name appears in the command itself, so you can read what will happen before pressing. Folders carry a trailing \, so they are distinguishable from files.

  • With archives selected — extraction
  • Extract... — opens a folder picker. Since you chose the destination yourself, the contents go straight into it
  • Extract here — puts the contents straight into the folder you are viewing
  • Extract to "(name)\" — creates a folder named after the archive and extracts into it (release.tar.gz gives you a release folder). If a folder of that name already exists, a new name is used, so contents never get mixed together. With several archives selected this becomes Extract each to its own folder
  • Extract to pane (A / B) — extracts into the folder open in the other pane, inside a folder named after the archive. No extracting and then copying. It is not shown when the other pane has no folder open

  • Test archive — reads the archive through to the end without writing a single byte, to tell you whether it is damaged. Use it when you want to know a download was truncated before extracting and littering your disk (see Detecting damage below). It appears only when ZIP or TAR files are selected (the Windows archive component offers no way to verify)

  • With anything else selected — compression

  • Compress... — opens a dialog for the destination folder and file name. The format can be ZIP, TAR, TAR.GZ or 7z (typing a name ending in .tar, .tar.gz or .7z picks that format too)
  • Compress to "(name).zip" — bundles the selection into one ZIP. The name comes from the single selected item, or from the current folder when several are selected
  • Compress to "(name).7z" — bundles it into a 7z with the same name. The 7z is made by the tar.exe that ships with Windows (present since the spring 2018 update to Windows 10). On Windows 11 it uses 7z's standard LZMA; on Windows 10, whose tar.exe has no LZMA, it uses the same method as ZIP (deflate). Either way 7-Zip and similar tools can open it. The strength follows the "ZIP compression level" setting below (Auto behaves like Standard for 7z). If a name contains characters that cannot be represented in the Windows code page (for example Korean or emoji on Japanese Windows), tar.exe cannot handle it, so no 7z is made and you are told which name it was. Compress as ZIP in that case
  • Compress each to its own ZIP — produces one ZIP per selected item (shown only with two or more selected)
  • Create ZIP in pane (A / B) — puts the resulting ZIP in the other pane's folder
  • Compress with level ▶ — makes the same ZIP as Compress to "(name).zip" (same place, same name), but with a different compression strength for this one time. The current default is checked
    • No compression (store only) — packs the files without shrinking them. The fastest choice; the size stays about the same as the originals. Suited to bundling photos and videos
    • Fastest / Standard / Smallest size — how much effort goes into shrinking. You choose a strength, not a target size (files that are already compressed barely shrink whichever you choose)
    • Auto (store photos, videos and the like as is) — stores formats that are already compressed (photos, videos, music, archives, Office documents and so on) as they are and shrinks the rest at Standard, so no time is spent on files that will not get smaller

The default strength for ZIPs made by Compress is set with "ZIP compression level" under Settings → General → File operations (it starts at Standard). All four compression entries above follow this default. It does not apply to TAR.GZ

  • Supported formats
Operation Formats How Extract ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ (.tgz) Built in (with safety checks; fast) Extract 7z / rar / TAR.BZ2 (.tbz2) / TAR.XZ (.txz) / TAR.ZST (.tzst) / single gz, bz2, xz, zst files Windows' archive folder (the same component behind File Explorer's "Extract All") Compress ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ (chosen in "Compress..."; the other entries make ZIP; ZIP also lets you choose the strength) Built in Compress 7z ("Compress..." or Compress to "(name).7z") The tar.exe that ships with Windows Extract rar (plus 7z, TAR.XZ, TAR.BZ2 and TAR.ZST when tar.exe has the components) On Windows without the archive folder support (such as Windows 10), the tar.exe that ships with Windows Extract 7z / TAR.XZ (.txz) / TAR.BZ2 (.tbz2) Only when neither the Windows archive folder nor tar.exe can read them (such as on Windows 10), a component built into the app (SharpCompress)

Reading 7z and rar is left to Windows wherever possible. The components that read them are large and complex, and serious vulnerabilities are found in them nearly every year; bundling one would make its vulnerabilities Zenith Filer's vulnerabilities. Instead, 7z, rar and the other formats are read by Windows' own archive component (the one File Explorer uses for "Extract All"), and the app handles only the destination, name clashes and undo. Windows Update keeps that component current. Windows decides which formats work (7z and rar arrived with the autumn 2023 update to Windows 11; on Windows 10 and other versions without that support, rar and others are extracted with the tar.exe that ships with Windows instead. The Windows 10 tar.exe cannot read 7z's standard compression (LZMA), tar.xz or tar.bz2, so those three alone are extracted with a component built into the app [SharpCompress]. It is written in .NET, which makes the memory-corruption kind of vulnerability found nearly every year in C and C++ components unlikely. It is used only when the Windows components cannot read the archive). It works even if your default app for those files is 7-Zip or another tool. CAB is excluded because Windows does not support extracting from it this way. Password-protected or damaged archives are reported as "Windows could not open this archive" with no dialog. Speed matches File Explorer's "Extract All" (around 30 seconds for 10,000 files; the built-in ZIP and TAR take a few seconds). Turning off "Use Windows to extract 7z, rar and other archives" under Settings → General → File operations returns to the built-in ZIP and TAR only. The built-in ZIP and TAR extraction uses only components that ship with Windows.

  • Safety rules: extracting means opening contents you did not write. These protections are always in effect.

  • Nothing is written outside the destination. The trick of slipping ..\ into a file name to write into a parent or system folder is blocked by resolving the real path and confirming it stays inside.

  • Shortcut (symbolic link) entries are discarded. Harmless-looking in themselves, they become the foothold that lets later files be written outside the destination.
  • An archive that expands abnormally is cut off part-way, so a small file cannot keep expanding until it fills the disk; extraction stops the moment more data arrives than the archive declared.
  • Windows reserved names such as CON and NUL, and alternate data streams hidden in a file name (readme.txt:other content), are not extracted.
  • The total extracted size is checked against the free space before anything is written.
  • For formats extracted by the Windows archive folder (7z, rar and so on), Windows itself drops entries that point outside the destination, and links fail. Windows will still create files with reserved names such as CON, so those are removed after extraction and reported by count. Stored checksums (CRC) cannot be verified
  • For formats extracted with tar.exe, tar.exe itself refuses entries that point outside the destination with .. or an absolute path (the refusals are reported by count). Files with reserved names and links are removed after extraction. When extracting into an existing folder, the archive is first extracted into a hidden staging folder inside it, then moved into place following your choices for name clashes (the staging folder is removed afterwards). Items whose names cannot be represented in the Windows code page cannot be read by tar.exe; they are skipped and reported
  • For formats extracted with the component built into the app (7z, tar.xz and tar.bz2 on Windows 10), entries are taken out one at a time under the same rules as ZIP and TAR: entries that point outside the destination, reserved names, alternate data streams and links are not written (and are reported by count). An archive that expands beyond 16 GB for one entry or 64 GB in total is cut off. Password-protected archives cannot be extracted. Extracting into an existing folder uses the same staging folder as tar.exe

Rejected entries are not discarded silently — the summary at the end reports "N unsafe entries were skipped".

  • Detecting damage: being readable and being intact are not the same thing. If the archive's structure survives, extraction goes through even when the data inside is corrupted, and a damaged file is left behind wearing a perfectly healthy name — the worst possible outcome. For ZIP, the contents are therefore checked during extraction against the checksum (CRC-32) recorded in the archive, and files that fail are removed rather than left behind, with the summary saying what went wrong. Test archive runs the same check without writing anything. Note that TAR and TAR.GZ carry no per-file checksum at all, so there the check can only confirm the archive's structure and, for gzip, that decompression succeeds.

  • When a name already exists: nothing is overwritten by default (the file is saved under a new name). If there are collisions you get the same confirmation used for copying, offering Replace, Skip or Keep both. Clear "Do the same for the remaining N" to decide one file at a time, and edit the name for Keep both.

  • Garbled names in older ZIPs: ZIPs created on Japanese Windows and similar systems may not store names in UTF-8. A ZIP without the UTF-8 marker is read using your system's code page, so names come out intact — the same behaviour as Explorer and 7-Zip.

  • Ctrl+Z puts it back. Undo removes only what this operation created. Files that were already there, and anything you placed in the folder yourself after extracting, are left alone.

  • Pricing: extracting is free. Compressing (creating ZIP, TAR, TAR.GZ or 7z) is limited to 3 times a day in the free version.

docs.title: Looking inside an archive
docs.text:
As when you open a zip in File Explorer, double-clicking an archive (or pressing Enter) opens it in the pane. This works for zip, 7z, rar, tar, tar.gz and other formats the app or Windows can extract (except CAB and the second and later parts of split archives).

  • Moving around inside: double-click a folder to go in; Backspace or a double-click on empty space goes up. Going up from the top of the archive returns to the folder that holds it, with the archive selected. The breadcrumb reads "… › archive name › folder inside".
  • Opening a file inside: double-clicking extracts it to a temporary folder and opens it in its default app (temporary folders are cleaned up after a day).
  • Getting files out: use the right-click "Extract..." (pick a destination) or "Extract to the (other) pane", or "Extract all..." on empty space. Ctrl+C puts the extracted files on the clipboard for another pane or File Explorer. Name conflicts get the same prompt as copying, and Ctrl+Z undoes it. You can also drag items out: they are first extracted to a temporary folder and, if you are still holding the button, carried as a copy (large files take a moment to extract; letting go while you wait does nothing; right-dragging cannot carry them).
  • Inside is read-only: delete, rename, paste, new items and drop are not available (you get a notice). Extract first if you want to change the contents.
  • Opening in the default app instead: hold Shift while double-clicking. To always use the default app, turn off "Open archives as folders on double-click" under Control Deck → "General" → "File operations" (on by default).
  • Password-protected archives either show nothing inside or say they could not be opened when you open a file. Use 7-Zip or similar for those.

docs.title: Text Comparison (Diff)
docs.text:
A feature that compares two text files side by side, highlighting the differences.

  • How to launch: From the right-click menu. There are two ways in, and both work in either pane:

    • Select two text files in the same pane and choose "Compare Text (in A pane)" ("in B pane" in the B pane)
    • Select one text file, with one text file also selected in the other pane, and choose "Compare Text (A ↔ B pane)"

  • What it handles: Text files up to 5 MB. The free version allows three comparisons a day.

  • Diff minimap: A minimap of the entire file's differences is displayed on the left edge of the screen, providing an overview of where changes are located. Click it to jump there.

  • Closing: Esc, or "Close" at the top right.

  • Synchronized scrolling: The left and right panels scroll in sync, keeping corresponding lines aligned side by side.

docs.title: Folder Comparison
docs.text:
Matches up the contents of the two folders open in pane A and pane B and lists where they differ. Open it with the "Compare folders (pane A and pane B)" button on the toolbar at the top of a pane. That button is not shown on the toolbar new users start with ("Fewer"). Set Settings → Toolbar → "Number of buttons" to "Standard" to show it (available in the free version too). The comparison itself is read-only and never modifies a file — nothing is written unless you run Make B match A from the result, described below.

  • Compare by: three choices.
  • Size only — the fastest
  • Size and modification time (default) — usually the right choice. Modification times within 2 seconds are treated as identical, because USB drives and NAS store timestamps at a coarser resolution and a strict comparison would mark every file as different

  • Contents (hash) — the most reliable, but it reads the whole file so it takes time. Only files of equal size are read, since a size difference already settles the matter

  • Reading the result: the marker at the start of each row shows the state. The shapes differ, so you never have to rely on colour alone.

Marker Meaning = Identical → Only on the left ← Only on the right Compare mark On both sides but the contents differ Case mark Only the letter case of the name differs

  • Identical items are hidden by default, because you came to look at the differences and showing everything buries them. Turn on Show identical items too to reveal them. The counts along the bottom always include them, so nothing is lost.

  • An exact one-hour gap is shown separately as a likely daylight-saving artefact. It is not treated as identical, but you can see that the contents are not actually different.

  • Names differing only in letter case are shown as their own state rather than silently treated as identical, since some environments handle them as two separate files. Turn on Case-sensitive names (off by default) and they are treated as different names instead, appearing as "only on the left" and "only on the right".

  • Include subfolders (on by default): turn it off to compare only the items directly inside the two open folders.

  • Exclusions: folders that tend to flood the result, such as node_modules and .git, are left out by default. Edit the list freely under Exclusions (one pattern per line; lines starting with # are comments).

  • Folders that could not be read: the comparison does not stop when permissions block a folder. It does not silently report zero either — it says "N folders could not be read" so you know the result is incomplete by that much.

  • Junctions and symbolic links are not followed, since following them can count the same file twice or loop forever.

docs.title: Bringing pane B into line with pane A
docs.text:
Once the comparison has shown you the differences, you can bring the pane B side into line with pane A without leaving the window. Use the Make B match A button on the result.

  • It is one-way. Only the pane B side changes; pane A is never modified. Two-way syncing would require deciding which side wins in every conflict, which makes the outcome impossible to predict in advance, so it is deliberately not offered.

  • The breakdown is shown before you press it. Next to the button you see "Syncing will: copy N, overwrite M, delete K", and you are asked to confirm once more before it runs. When there is nothing to do, the button cannot be pressed.

  • Items that exist only on the right are not deleted by default, because deletion is the mistake the word "sync" invites most easily. To remove them, tick Delete items only on the right. The delete count in the breakdown updates immediately, so you can always check the number before pressing.

  • Ctrl+Z puts it back. Overwriting and deleting cannot be taken back on their own, so the original files are moved to a backup folder before the run — a single undo reverts everything the sync did (copied files disappear again; overwritten and deleted files come back with their contents). Five generations of backups are kept under folder_sync_backup in the app's data folder, with the oldest cleaned up automatically.

  • A failure does not stop the run. If a file cannot be opened or written, the rest still goes through and the number of failures is reported at the end. Only what succeeded is included in the undo.

  • Only files are synced. Folders themselves are not transferred, but the parent folders needed at the destination are created automatically.

  • Comparing is free; the sync is limited to 3 uses a day in the free version.

docs.title: Connecting to a Server (FTP / SFTP)
docs.text:
Folders on a server open in a pane just like folders on your PC, so you can move things back and forth in the usual two-pane layout without launching a separate transfer program.

You register servers and test connections in the Sites view in the navigation pane (see Nav pane); once a folder is open, working with it is much the same as working locally. The Sites view is not on the icon bar at first: place it with the cross-shaped layout window, or with the "Zenith 2" keymap press Ctrl+K then N (opening it also adds it to the icon bar). You can also register a server by typing sftp://… into the address bar (see below).

  • Registering a server: Give it a name, host, port, user name, authentication method (password or private key), and an initial folder. Leave the port blank to use the default for the protocol you picked (22 for SFTP, 21 for FTP, 990 for FTPS). Leave the display name blank and the host name is used as-is; leave the user name blank and FTP connects anonymously. The button at the bottom runs a connection test so you can confirm it works right there.

  • Opening a folder: Double-click a row in the Sites view, or use the open-folder button, and the server's folder appears in the active pane. Opening folders, going up a level, and jumping to a level from the breadcrumb all work as they do locally. The right-click menu can open it too.

  • You can always tell which pane is remote — the connection (user@host) appears at the start of the breadcrumb, so there is no operating on a server while believing you are local.

  • Downloading: Select files on the server side and copy them to the other pane. Whole folders can be brought over at once. Progress is shown along the bottom of the window.

  • Working on the server: You can upload, delete, rename, and create folders. The operations are the same as local ones, but deleting and uploading on the server cannot be undone with Ctrl+Z — servers have nothing like a Recycle Bin, so there is no way to bring back something that has been deleted (renaming is the exception: Ctrl+Z reverts it). Deletions ask for confirmation first. A "move" to or from a server is carried out as a copy, so the original stays where it was.

  • Permissions: File and folder permissions on the server can be changed from the right-click menu.

  • Character encoding: FTP servers differ in how they encode file names. If names come out garbled, set the encoding on the registration screen. (SFTP is always UTF-8, so there is nothing to set.)

  • How your credentials are handled

  • Passwords and passphrases are stored so that only this Windows user can decrypt them. Carrying the settings file to another PC or user account will not decrypt, and you will be asked to enter them again.

  • Private keys are not copied — only their location is remembered. Duplicating key material just creates more copies to hunt down and delete later.
  • On the first SFTP connection the host key fingerprint is shown for you to approve, and the approved fingerprint is recorded. If a different key turns up later, the connection is stopped. It may only mean the server was rebuilt, but it can also mean the destination has been substituted, and only you can tell those apart.
  • FTPS certificates are verified, and there is no setting to accept them unconditionally.

  • Connections are opened when you actually use them and closed automatically after a period of inactivity (nothing happens at startup, and a connection in the middle of a transfer is never dropped).

  • Where it differs from local folders: files on a server do not exist on this PC, which leads to the following differences.

Folders on a server Icons The standard ones, decided by name and extension Thumbnails Not fetched (each one would trigger a download) Picking up changes made by other programs Not done — refresh manually Opening by double-click Not available — bring the file to your PC first Undo (Ctrl+Z) Not for deletes and uploads (renames can be undone)

A failed connection is never shown as an empty folder. The reason is always displayed.

docs.title: The Sites view and working in a pane
docs.text:
• Sites View: Register SFTP, FTP, and FTPS servers and verify that they connect.

    Each row shows the server name and its address in sftp://user@host form. The icon at the start of the row distinguishes encrypted connections (SFTP / FTPS) from plain FTP.

    The buttons along the bottom open, add, edit, test, and delete entries. Double-clicking a row opens it in the pane you are working in.

    Right-click menu: Right-clicking a row offers "Open in pane / Open in pane A / Open in pane B / Edit site / Test connection / Delete". The row you right-clicked becomes the selected one. Right-clicking empty space offers "Add site / Refresh list".

    Registering from the address bar: You do not have to open this view at all — type sftp://user@host/path straight into a pane's address bar.

    • If the connection is not registered yet, "Add site" opens with what you typed already filled in (protocol, host, port, user and folder). Enter the password, save, and that folder opens.
    • If it is registered, it just opens.
    • If the form cannot be read, the app tells you which part it could not read (how the port is written, a missing host, a password that cannot go in an address, and so on).

    • Type three characters or more and any saved connection whose name, host or address matches appears below as a suggestion. Press ↓ to move into the list and Enter, or click, to open it; Esc closes the list.

    • Passwords and passphrases are stored so that only this Windows user can decrypt them. Settings carried over to another PC or user account cannot be decrypted, so you will need to re-enter them there.

    • Private keys are never copied — only the file location is remembered.
    • Leaving Port empty uses the standard port for the selected protocol (22 for SFTP, 21 for FTP, 990 for FTPS).
    • Leaving Display name empty uses the host name as the name.
    • Leaving User name empty connects as anonymous FTP.

    Host key check: The first time you connect over SFTP, the fingerprint the server presented is shown for your approval. Confirm that it matches the one your administrator gave you before approving. The approved fingerprint is recorded and you will not be asked again. If a key ever differs from the recorded one, the connection is stopped — the server may simply have been rebuilt, but the connection may also have been redirected to another machine. If you have no reason to expect the change, do not connect.

    Opening in a pane: Double-click a row, or use the open button, and the server's folder appears in the pane you are working in. Entering folders, going up a level (Backspace), and jumping to a level from the breadcrumb work just as they do for local folders.

    A pane showing a remote folder is marked in three ways:

    • The tab icon becomes a server icon.
    • A protocol badge (SFTP / FTP / FTPS) appears at the start of the address bar.
    • The pane gets an accent-colored outline.
